title: Two clues, two unknowns
objectives: Solve simultaneous equations by adding or subtracting them to remove one letter
Scale a whole equation so one letter matches before removing it

screens.prose: Two cinema orders at the same prices. The first is 2 tickets and a drink for £11.00. The second is 3 tickets and a drink for £15.00.

state.caption: T is a ticket and D is a drink. Every ticket costs the same.

screens.question: What does one ticket cost?

hints.text: What does the second order have that the first does not?
Line the orders up. The second has one ticket more.
That extra ticket is the only difference, so it costs £15.00 − £11.00.

feedback.correct: The second order is the first plus one ticket, and it costs £4.00 more.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the two orders item by item.

byKey.all-tickets: You shared £15.00 between the 3 tickets. The drink is part of that £15.00, so each ticket costs less.
byKey.half-first: You shared £11.00 between the 2 tickets. The drink is part of that £11.00 too.
byKey.per-item: You shared both bills over all seven items. A drink and a ticket need not cost the same.

explain.text: You compared the orders. Everything in the first is also in the second, except one ticket. So that ticket accounts for the whole £4.00 difference.

screens.prose: A third order at the same prices: 4 tickets and a drink for £19.00. Tap items in the third order to mark them. Tap again to clear.

state.caption: Match each item in the first order with one in the third.

screens.question: Mark the items in the third order that the first order does not have.

hints.text: Pair each item in the first order with a matching item in the third.
The first order has one drink and two tickets.
After pairing, two tickets in the third order have no partner. Mark any two tickets.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match off everything the two orders share, then mark what is left.

byKey.cd: Both orders have one drink, so the drink is not extra. It pairs with the drink in the first order.
byKey.too-many: You marked more than the extras. Two of the four tickets pair with the two in the first order.
byKey.too-few: One extra is not all of it. The first order has two tickets and the third has four.

explain.text: You matched two tickets and the drink, and two tickets were left. Those two cost £19.00 − £11.00 = £8.00, so £4.00 each. That agrees with the last screen.

screens.prose: Back to the first two orders. You know a ticket costs £4.00.
screens.question: What does the drink cost?

hints.text: Pick one order. What do its tickets cost together?
The first order has two tickets at £4.00 each.
Two tickets cost £8.00. The drink is the rest of the £11.00.

feedback.correct: Two tickets make £8.00, and the drink is the other £3.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the cost of all the tickets away from the order's total.

byKey.one-ticket: You took one ticket off £11.00. The first order has two tickets, so take off £8.00.
byKey.second-one: You took one ticket off £15.00. The second order has three tickets, so take off £12.00.

explain.text: Two tickets at £4.00 make £8.00, so the drink is £11.00 − £8.00 = £3.00. Check with the second order: $3 \times 4 + 3 = 15$. Both orders agree.

screens.prose: Write $t$ for the ticket price and $d$ for the drink, in pounds. The orders say $2t + d = 11$ and $3t + d = 15$. Two equations that share their unknowns are called **simultaneous equations**.
screens.question: Solve them as you did with the orders: get rid of $d$ first. Tap a step.

ops.label: Subtract the first equation from the second
Add the two equations
ops.why: You added the equations, so the drinks piled up to $2d$. Both have $+d$, so subtracting removes it.

hints.text: With the orders, you matched off the drink. Which step does that to the equations?
Both equations hold exactly one $d$.
Subtract the first equation from the second. The $d$ terms cancel and leave $t = 4$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Remove $d$ first, then find $t$, then $d$.

byKey.m-add: You added the equations, so $d + d = 2d$ stayed in. Both have $+d$, so subtracting removes it.

explain.text: Subtracting the equations did on paper what you did with the orders: it matched off the shared items. The $d$ terms cancel because both are $+d$. This method is called **elimination**: remove one unknown, solve for the other.

screens.prose: A new pair. The table lines the equations up term by term. This time the $y$ terms have opposite signs.
screens.question: Remove $y$, then solve. Tap a step.

ops.label: Subtract the first equation from the second
ops.why: You subtracted, so the $y$ terms became $-2y - 2y = -4y$. Opposite signs cancel when you add.

hints.text: Look at the signs of the two $y$ terms.
One is $+2y$ and the other is $-2y$.
$+2y$ and $-2y$ add to nothing. Add the equations: $8x = 32$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Choose the step that makes the $y$ terms cancel.

byKey.m-sub: You subtracted, so the $y$ terms became $-4y$. Opposite signs cancel when you add.

explain.text: $+2y$ and $-2y$ add to zero, so adding removed $y$ and left $8x = 32$. Then $12 + 2y = 16$ gives $y = 2$. Same signs, subtract; opposite signs, add.

screens.prose: A café: 4 coffees and 2 croissants cost £13.00. 2 coffees and 3 croissants cost £10.50. Write $c$ and $k$ for the prices. No letter matches yet.
screens.question: Make one letter match, remove it, and solve. Tap a step.

ops.label: Subtract the second equation from the first
ops.why: You subtracted before any terms matched, so both letters were left. Make one letter match first.

ops.label: Double the left side of the second equation
ops.why: You doubled the left side only, so the second equation became false. Double the 10.5 too.

ops.label: Add the two equations
ops.why: Both $c$ terms are $+4c$, so adding gave $8c$. Subtract to remove them.

ops.label: Subtract the first equation from the second

hints.text: Can you make the coffee terms equal by scaling one whole equation?
$2c$ doubled is $4c$, the same as in the first equation.
Double every term of the second equation: $4c + 6k = 21$. Then subtract the first.

feedback.correct: A coffee costs £2.25 and a croissant £2.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Scale a whole equation so one letter matches, then remove it.

byKey.m-half: You doubled the left side only. The equation stays true only if the 10.5 doubles too.
byKey.m-add: Both $c$ terms were $+4c$, so adding doubled them. Subtract to remove them.
byKey.m-early: You subtracted before any letter matched, so both letters were left over.

explain.text: Doubling the whole second equation made the coffees match: $4c$ in both. That is allowed because both sides double, so it stays true. Subtracting then left $4k = 8$, so $k = 2$ and $c = 2.25$.

screens.prose: Two baskets of shares at fixed prices. 5 of P and 2 of Q cost £31.50. 3 of P and 2 of Q cost £20.50. Write $p$ and $q$ for the prices.
screens.question: Subtract the second equation from the first. Which line do you get?

options.why: You subtracted the left sides but kept 31.5 on the right. The right side loses 20.5 too.
You added the equations. Both have $+2q$, so adding doubles $q$ instead of removing it.
You subtracted the left sides but added the right sides. Each side must have the same thing done to it.

hints.text: Subtracting one equation from another means subtracting on both sides.
Work down each column: first row minus second row.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the second row from the first in every column, including the totals.

byKey.left-only: You took $3p + 2q$ from the left but kept 31.5 on the right. The left lost £20.50 worth of shares, so the right must lose 20.5 too.
byKey.added: You added the equations. Both have $+2q$, so adding doubles $q$ instead of removing it.

explain.text: Subtracting equations means subtracting both sides: $(5p + 2q) - (3p + 2q) = 31.5 - 20.5$. That gives $2p = 11$, so $p = 5.5$ and then $q = 2$. A share of P costs £5.50 and Q £2.00.

screens.prose: Each time, you made one letter's terms equal in size, then combined the equations to remove it. $$\text{same sign: subtract} \qquad \text{opposite signs: add}$$ $$(3t + d) - (2t + d) = 15 - 11 \quad \Rightarrow \quad t = 4$$ Whatever you do, do it to both sides.
screens.question: To remove $y$ from $4x + 3y = 18$ and $x - 3y = -3$, what do you do?

options.text: Subtract the second equation from the first
options.why: The $y$ terms have opposite signs. Subtracting gives $3y - (-3y) = 6y$, which keeps $y$.

options.text: Take $3y$ from both sides of the first equation
options.why: That moves $y$ around inside one equation. To remove it, combine the two equations.

options.text: Multiply the second equation by 4, then subtract
options.why: That makes the $x$ terms match, so it removes $x$, not $y$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the signs of the two $y$ terms.

explain.text: $+3y$ and $-3y$ have opposite signs, so adding removes them: $5x = 15$. Then $x = 3$, and $3 - 3y = -3$ gives $y = 2$. Check: $12 + 6 = 18$.

screens.prose: Solve $3m + 2n = 23$ and $m + 2n = 13$ by elimination. Each line carries its reason.
screens.question: Put the lines of the solution in order.

lines.text: $(3m + 2n) - (m + 2n) = 23 - 13$, subtract the second equation from the first: both have $+2n$
$n = 4$, take 5 from both sides, then halve

hints.text: Which letter has matching terms? Removing it comes first.
Subtract to remove $n$, solve for $m$, put $m$ back to find $n$, then check.

feedback.correct: $m = 5$ and $n = 4$, checked in the other equation.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Remove a letter first, then solve, substitute back and check.

byKey.o4: You put a value of $m$ back in before finding it. Solve $2m = 10$ first.

explain.text: Both equations have $+2n$, so subtracting removes $n$ and gives $2m = 10$. Putting $m = 5$ back gives $n = 4$. The check uses the equation you did not substitute into.

screens.prose: Two trades at the same fixed prices. Your statement: 3 shares of X and 2 of Y for £62.50. A colleague's: 5 of X and 2 of Y for £92.50.
screens.question: What is the price of one share of Y?

widget.label: Price of one share of Y

hints.text: Which share appears the same number of times in both?
Both bought 2 of Y. Subtract the statements.
2 shares of X cost £30.00, so X is £15.00. Then $3 \times 15 + 2y = 62.5$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the statements to find X, then put it back to find Y.

byKey.x-price: That is the price of X. Put it back into your statement to find Y.
byKey.no-x: You shared £62.50 between the 2 shares of Y. The 3 shares of X are in that total too.
byKey.difference: £30.00 is the cost of the 2 extra shares of X. It gives X, not Y.

explain.text: Subtracting the statements removes Y: $2x = 30$, so $x = 15$. Then $45 + 2y = 62.5$ gives $y = 8.75$. Check: $5 \times 15 + 2 \times 8.75 = 92.5$.

ideas: Two unknowns need two facts. Line the equations up so one letter's terms match in size.
Same sign: subtract the equations. Opposite signs: add them. Either way, both sides take part.
Solve for the letter that is left, put it back into one equation, and check in the other.

formula.name: Elimination
formula.tex: (a_1x + by) - (a_2x + by) = c_1 - c_2 \quad \Rightarrow \quad (a_1 - a_2)x = c_1 - c_2
formula.note: The matching $by$ terms cancel. Scale a whole equation first if nothing matches.

summary.trap: Subtract the right sides as well as the left. If the matching terms have the same sign, adding doubles them instead of removing them.

quiz.prose: Two numbers satisfy $x + y = 12$ and $x - y = 2$.
quiz.question: What is $x$?

options.why: That is $y$. Adding the equations gives $2x = 14$, so $x = 7$.
You added the equations to get $2x = 14$, then stopped. Divide by 2.
You halved 12 and ignored the second equation. $x$ is 2 more than $y$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the equations to remove $y$.

explain.text: The $y$ terms have opposite signs, so adding removes them: $2x = 14$, $x = 7$. Then $y = 5$. Check: $7 - 5 = 2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract to remove $b$, find $a$, then put it back.

byKey.a: That is $a$. Put $a = 4$ back into either equation to find $b$.
byKey.two-a: $8$ is $2a$, from subtracting. Halve it to get $a$, then find $b$.

explain.text: Both have $+3b$, so subtract: $2a = 8$, $a = 4$. Then $8 + 3b = 17$ gives $b = 3$. Check: $16 + 9 = 25$.

quiz.prose: One till says 2 tickets and a drink cost £11.00. Another till, at the same prices, says 2 tickets and a drink cost £12.00.
quiz.question: What can you say about the prices?

options.text: No ticket and drink prices fit both tills

options.why: You subtracted and read $0 = 1$ as $t = 1$. Both letters vanished, and $0 = 1$ is false.
You averaged the two totals. No pair of prices can make the same order cost two amounts.
That happens when two facts say the same thing. These two facts contradict each other.

feedback.correct: The same order cannot cost two amounts.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the equations and look at what is left.

explain.text: Subtracting $2t + d = 11$ from $2t + d = 12$ gives $0 = 1$, which is false. So no prices fit both. One till is wrong, or the prices changed.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The $y$ terms have opposite signs, so add.

byKey.x: That is $x$. Put $x = 5$ back to find $y$.

explain.text: Adding removes $y$: $5x = 25$, so $x = 5$. Then $10 + 5y = 20$ gives $y = 2$. Check: $15 - 10 = 5$.
